decision_scope: Rank migration-critical workflow families for a v0.1 product that supports one owner in one workspace and one team while covering varied project types.

method.discovery: General web search through AnySearch, followed by direct verification against official publisher pages and reports.
inclusion: Official primary publication or official report page
At least 2,000 survey respondents or large product telemetry
Published sample and coverage information sufficient to identify the represented population
A statistic relevant to work tracking, project method, information retrieval, tool consolidation, usability, security, cost, or open-source preference
exclusion: SEO summaries and unsourced market-size estimates
Small qualitative studies and individual interviews
Statistics that cannot be verified on an official publisher surface

sources.title: 2025 Developer Survey
sources.sample: More than 49,000 respondents in 177 countries overall; relevant questions contain 8,758 to 35,897 responses.
sources.coverage: Professional, learning, work, personal, and school software projects; tool use, tool count, purchase criteria, and rejection criteria.
statistics_used: Among 30,065 respondents to the collaboration-tool question, GitHub was used by 81%, Jira by 46%, and GitLab by 36%.
Among 27,378 respondents, 54% used at least six software applications or platforms for work.
Among 25,391 respondents, 65% used five or fewer tools for side or personal projects.
Among 23,603 work-project responses, security or privacy was the first-ranked rejection reason, pricing second, poor usability fourth, and time cost fifth.
Among 8,758 personal-project responses, pricing was first and security or privacy second among rejection reasons.
AI integration ranked ninth of ten endorsement attributes for both work and personal projects.
limitations: The survey is self-selected and centered on people who code.
Tool use does not identify which workflow inside a tool is valued.
Question-level response counts differ and percentages are not a migration-intent measure.
sources.conflict_of_interest: Stack Overflow publishes collaboration products, but the survey data and question counts are public; vendor influence is retained as a limitation.

sources.title: Pulse of the Profession 2024: The Future of Project Work
sources.sample: 2,246 project professionals and 342 senior leaders worldwide.
sources.coverage: Government, IT, financial services, telecommunications, energy, manufacturing, healthcare, construction, and other industries across seven world regions.
statistics_used: Respondents reporting always or often use were 43.9% predictive, 31.5% hybrid, and 24.6% agile; respondents could select more than one approach.
Hybrid use rose from 20% in 2020 to 31.5% in 2023, a 57% increase.
Seventy-six percent expected agile use and 73% expected hybrid use to increase over the following five years.
Overall reported project performance was 73.8%, with comparable results across predictive, hybrid, and agile approaches.
limitations: The sample represents project professionals and leaders rather than only software teams or current Linear users.
Method prevalence supports a method-neutral model but does not select individual application controls.
sources.conflict_of_interest: PMI publishes project-management standards and credentials; the report methodology and population are disclosed.

sources.title: 2024 Global DevSecOps Report
sources.sample: More than 5,000 software development, security, and operations professionals in 39 countries.
sources.coverage: DevSecOps roles and multiple industries, including public sector, financial services, telecommunications, automotive, and manufacturing.
statistics_used: Sixty-four percent wanted to consolidate their toolchain.
Sixty-seven percent reported that their software-development lifecycle was mostly or completely automated.
limitations: The survey is vendor-maintainered and promotes an integrated platform category.
Toolchain consolidation is not direct evidence for any single issue-tracker feature.
sources.conflict_of_interest: GitLab directly benefits from platform-consolidation conclusions; this source is never used alone for a priority score.

sources.title: State of Teams 2024
sources.sample: 5,000 knowledge workers, 100 Fortune 500 executives, product data from 1 million Atlassian users, and 24 million Jira tickets.
sources.coverage: United States, Australia, India, Germany, and France; equal survey split across work management, IT service management, and DevOps; 60% small and medium businesses and 40% enterprise organizations.
statistics_used: Seventy percent of knowledge workers said fewer, more specific goals would make progress easier.
Fifty-five percent found information hard to locate even when they knew relevant people.
Fifty-six percent said inconsistent planning and tracking approaches made collaboration difficult.
Fifty percent had discovered that another team was working on the same project only after work had begun.
The reported high-performing-team cohort was 1.6 times more likely to plan and track work consistently.
limitations: The survey is vendor-maintainered and team-oriented, while v0.1 exposes one owner.
The public page does not publish enough detail to independently reproduce every cohort calculation.
Team-collaboration findings support information architecture, not multi-user scope for v0.1.
sources.conflict_of_interest: Atlassian sells work-management products; its findings are triangulated with Stack Overflow, PMI, and GitLab and are not treated as independent product-performance evidence.

coverage_assessment.additional_product_telemetry: 1 million platform users and 24 million Jira tickets
coverage_assessment.non_independence_note: Totals are descriptive lower bounds, not a pooled statistical sample; sources have different frames and may overlap.
